Abies alba.note: The silver fir of the European mountain forests.

Acacia aneura.note: Mulga, the wattle whose upswept leaves funnel rain to its own trunk; it covers a fifth of the continent.

Acanthogammarus.note: Armoured, spiny amphipods: part of a species flock of over 350 amphipods found only in Lake Baikal.

Acer saccharum.note: The sugar maple, which with beech forms the climax forest of the north-eastern hills.

Acinonyx jubatus.note: The cheetah, fastest land animal, a sprinter of open ground.

Acipenser fulvescens.note: The lake sturgeon: armoured, bottom-feeding, living past a hundred years in the Great Lakes and Hudson Bay rivers.

Adansonia grandidieri.note: Grandidier's baobab, the smooth grey giants of the Avenue of the Baobabs. Six of the eight baobab species are Madagascan.

Agathis australis.note: Kauri, the giant of the northern New Zealand forest, its trunks five metres through.

Agave.note: Century plants: rosette succulents that flower once, on a mast several metres tall, and die.

Alcolapia.note: Soda tilapias living in 40-degree, pH 10 springs at the edge of Lakes Natron and Magadi.

Allactaga.note: Jerboas: hopping desert rodents with kangaroo legs and tufted tails.

Alligator mississippiensis.note: The American alligator, engineer of the south-eastern swamps, whose 'gator holes' hold water through drought.

Aloidendron dichotomum.note: The quiver tree: a giant tree-aloe of the Namib edge, now dying back at the hot end of its range.

Alouatta.note: Howler monkeys, whose dawn roar carries five kilometres through the forest.

Amblyrhynchus cristatus.note: The marine iguana, the only lizard that forages in the sea, grazing algae off Galapagos reefs.

Ammotragus lervia.note: The Barbary sheep or aoudad of the Saharan massifs and the Atlas.

Andrias davidianus.note: The Chinese giant salamander, up to 1.8 m, the largest living amphibian.

Antidorcas marsupialis.note: The springbok, once migrating across the Karoo and Kalahari in herds of millions.

Aphanius.note: Killifish of salt springs and desert pools around the Mediterranean and Arabia, tolerant of brine saltier than the sea.

Aquila chrysaetos.note: The golden eagle, hunting open mountain country around the whole northern hemisphere.

Ara.note: Macaws, the great long-tailed parrots that gather at riverbank clay licks.

Araucaria araucana.note: The monkey puzzle of the southern Andes, a Jurassic-looking conifer that can live a thousand years.

Artemisia tridentata.note: Big sagebrush, the grey-green shrub that defines the cold deserts of the intermountain West.

Arthrospira.note: Spirulina: the coiled cyanobacterium that turns soda lakes green and the flamingos pink.

Babyrousa.note: The babirusa of Sulawesi, whose upper tusks grow up through the snout and curl back toward the skull.

Bertholletia excelsa.note: The Brazil nut tree, a fifty-metre emergent that only one large bee can pollinate and only the agouti can plant.

Birgus latro.note: The coconut crab, a metre across: the largest land arthropod, a hermit crab that gave up its shell.

Bison bonasus.note: The wisent, Europe's forest bison, saved from a dozen zoo animals.

Bootherium bombifrons.note: The helmeted muskox, a taller, woodland relative of the living muskox, found only in Ice Age North America.

Bos gaurus.note: The gaur, largest of wild cattle, of Indian and Indochinese hill forest.

Boselaphus tragocamelus.note: The nilgai or blue bull, the largest Asian antelope.

Boswellia sacra.note: The frankincense tree of Dhofar and Somalia, growing from bare rock and bled for its resin for five thousand years.

Bradypus.note: Three-toed sloths, hanging in the canopy and descending once a week.

Bubo scandiacus.note: The snowy owl, a daytime hunter of lemmings on open tundra.

Buceros.note: The great hornbills, seed-dispersers of the Asian rainforest, the female sealed into the nest hole.

Camelus dromedarius.note: The one-humped camel of Arabia and the Sahara, able to lose a third of its body water and drink it back in minutes.

Capra aegagrus.note: The bezoar or wild goat of the Zagros and Taurus, ancestor of the domestic goat.

Capra caucasica.note: The Caucasian tur, a heavy-horned ibex found only on the Greater Caucasus.

Carnegiea gigantea.note: The saguaro: a column cactus of the Sonoran Desert that takes seventy years to grow its first arm.

Castor canadensis.note: The North American beaver, whose dams engineered the continent's stream valleys.

Casuarius casuarius.note: The southern cassowary, a helmeted rainforest bird that swallows fruit whole and plants the forest.

Cedrus atlantica.note: The Atlas cedar, forming the high forests of Morocco and Algeria.

Centrocercus urophasianus.note: The greater sage-grouse, displaying on ancestral leks in the sagebrush sea.

Cervalces scotti.note: The stag-moose: a moose-sized deer with elaborate palmate antlers, living in the spruce bogs at the ice margin.

Chelonoidis niger.note: The Galapagos giant tortoise, each island with its own shell shape -- one of the observations that started Darwin thinking.

Chinchilla.note: Chinchillas of the high, dry Andes, carrying the densest fur of any land mammal.

Chionochloa.note: Snow tussocks, the tall bunch grasses of the New Zealand high country.

Cocos nucifera.note: The coconut palm, spread by its own floating seeds to every tropical shore.

Colobanthus quitensis.note: Antarctic pearlwort, one of only two flowering plants native to Antarctica.

Comephorus.note: Golomyanka: translucent, scaleless Baikal fish, a third oil by weight, bearing live young in open water.

Copiapoa.note: Globular cacti of the Atacama coast that live on fog: some stands see no rain for decades.

Coregonus migratorius.note: The omul, the whitefish on which Lake Baikal's fishery has always rested.

Cortaderia selloana.note: Pampas grass, three-metre tussocks with silver plumes.

Crocodylus niloticus.note: The Nile crocodile, top predator of African rivers and lakes.

Crocodylus porosus.note: The saltwater crocodile, largest living reptile, crossing open sea between estuaries.

Crocuta crocuta.note: The spotted hyena: a hunter as much as a scavenger, living in female-led clans. Ice Age Europe had it too, as the cave hyena.

Crotalus.note: Rattlesnakes, a New World invention: pit vipers with a warning rattle of interlocking keratin.

Cyathea dealbata.note: The silver fern, a tree fern whose fronds shine white beneath.

Dacrydium cupressinum.note: Rimu, the weeping podocarp that towers over New Zealand's lowland rainforest.

Daubentonia madagascariensis.note: The aye-aye, tapping on wood and fishing out grubs with one skeletal finger -- Madagascar's woodpecker.

Davidia involucrata.note: The dove tree, a relict of the Tertiary forests of the northern hemisphere surviving in the mountains of Sichuan.

Deinacrida.note: Giant weta: flightless crickets heavier than a sparrow, filling the role mice play elsewhere.

Dendrolagus.note: Tree-kangaroos: kangaroos that went back up into the rainforest canopy.

Dendrosenecio.note: Giant groundsels, tree-sized daisies of the East African summits, each mountain with its own species.

Diceros bicornis.note: The black rhinoceros, a hook-lipped browser of thorn scrub.

Dolichotis patagonum.note: The mara: a long-legged, hare-like cavy of the Patagonian scrub that pairs for life.

Drepanidinae.note: Hawaiian honeycreepers: one finch colonist radiated into over fifty species with bills for every job. Most are now extinct.

Dromaius novaehollandiae.note: The emu, nomadic across the whole continent, walking hundreds of kilometres after rain.

Dryas octopetala.note: Mountain avens, the tundra mat-plant whose leaves in lake mud named the Younger Dryas cold snap.

Elaphurus davidianus.note: Pere David's deer, a swamp deer of the Chinese lowlands, extinct in the wild and saved in an English park.

Equus hemionus.note: The onager or kulan, the wild ass of the Asian deserts, able to run at 70 km/h.

Equus kiang.note: The kiang, the wild ass of the Tibetan Plateau.

Equus quagga.note: The plains zebra, migrating with the wildebeest.

Equus zebra.note: The mountain zebra of the Cape ranges and the Namibian escarpment.

Eriophorum.note: Cottongrass, whitening Arctic bogs in summer and building the tussocks of the tundra.

Espeletia.note: Frailejones, the woolly giant rosettes of the paramo, wrapped in their own dead leaves against nightly frost.

Eunectes murinus.note: The green anaconda, heaviest of all snakes, an ambush hunter of swamp and slow river.

Ficus benghalensis.note: The banyan, a strangler fig that spreads on aerial roots until one tree is a grove.

Fitzroya cupressoides.note: The alerce, a giant cypress of the Valdivian rainforest; one tree is over 3,600 years old.

Furcifer.note: Chameleons: half of all species live on Madagascar.

Gavialis gangeticus.note: The gharial, a fish-eating crocodilian of the Ganges and Indus systems with a snout like a pair of pliers.

Gazella.note: Gazelles: small, fast antelopes of open arid country from Morocco to India.

Gazella subgutturosa.note: The goitered gazelle of the Gobi and the Iranian plateau.

Giraffa camelopardalis.note: The giraffe, browsing acacia crowns five metres up.

Goliathus.note: Goliath beetles, among the heaviest insects, feeding on sap and fruit in African forest canopies.

Gopherus agassizii.note: The desert tortoise, digging burrows that dozens of other desert animals depend on.

Gypaetus barbatus.note: The bearded vulture or lammergeier, which lives on bones and drops them on rocks to break them.

Hagenia abyssinica.note: The kosso tree of the African mountain forests, up to the edge of the moorland.

Haliaeetus leucocephalus.note: The bald eagle, a fish eagle of North American lakes, rivers and coasts.

Haloxylon.note: Saxaul: leafless, salt-tolerant small trees that are the only woodland the Central Asian deserts have.

Haplochromine cichlids.note: Hundreds of cichlid species evolved inside single African lakes -- in Lake Victoria, in perhaps fifteen thousand years.

Heloderma suspectum.note: The Gila monster, a venomous lizard that spends nine tenths of its life underground.

Homo floresiensis.note: The 'hobbit' of Flores: a metre-tall hominin with a chimpanzee-sized brain, making stone tools beside dwarf elephants.

Huso huso.note: The beluga sturgeon of the Caspian and Black Sea basins, up to a tonne and a century old.

Hyaena hyaena.note: The striped hyena, a solitary scavenger of dry country from the Sahel to India.

Hydrochoerus hydrochaeris.note: The capybara, the largest living rodent, grazing in herds at the water's edge.

Lagopus.note: Ptarmigan: grouse with feathered feet, white in winter and mottled in summer.

Lama guanicoe.note: The guanaco, wild ancestor of the llama, from sea-level Patagonian steppe to the high Atacama.

Larrea.note: Creosote bush and jarilla: resinous desert shrubs of both Americas, whose clonal rings in the Mojave are among the oldest living things.

Lates niloticus.note: The Nile perch, a two-metre predator of the Nile, Chad and Congo systems.

Lavigeria.note: Heavily armoured Tanganyikan snails that look marine, shaped by an arms race with shell-crushing crabs.

Leiopelma.note: New Zealand's native frogs: no eardrums, no croak, no tadpoles -- little changed since the Jurassic.

Leontopodium nivale.note: Edelweiss, felted white against ultraviolet light on Alpine limestone.

Leptonychotes weddellii.note: The Weddell seal, the southernmost mammal, keeping breathing holes open in fast ice with its teeth.

Lepus arcticus.note: The Arctic hare, white year-round in the far north, gathering in flocks of hundreds.

Leucogeranus leucogeranus.note: The Siberian crane, breeding on Arctic wetlands and wintering five thousand kilometres south.

Liolaemus.note: Over 250 species of small lizards from Patagonia to the high Andes -- one of the largest lizard radiations anywhere.

Loxodonta cyclotis.note: The forest elephant, smaller and straighter-tusked, whose trails and seed dispersal shape the Congo forest.

Lubomirskia baicalensis.note: A branching green freshwater sponge forming metre-high underwater forests on Baikal's rocky slopes.

Lycalopex culpaeus.note: The culpeo, a fox-like South American canid of the Andes and the Patagonian steppe.

Lynx lynx.note: The Eurasian lynx, ambush hunter of roe deer in forest and mountain.

Macaca fuscata.note: The Japanese macaque, the northernmost-living monkey, warming itself in hot springs.

Macaca sylvanus.note: The Barbary macaque of the Atlas cedar forests, the only monkey north of the Sahara; in the Pleistocene it ranged to England.

Mandrillus sphinx.note: The mandrill, the largest monkey, of the rainforests around the Gulf of Guinea.

Martes zibellina.note: The sable, whose fur drove the Russian conquest of Siberia.

Megadyptes antipodes.note: The yellow-eyed penguin, nesting alone in coastal forest rather than in colonies.

Melanosuchus niger.note: The black caiman, five metres long, the largest predator of the Amazon basin.

Moloch horridus.note: The thorny devil: an ant-eating lizard whose skin channels dew to its mouth.

Monodon monoceros.note: The narwhal, whose spiral tusk is a single tooth carrying millions of nerve endings.

Moschus moschiferus.note: The Siberian musk deer: antlerless, with sabre-like canines.

Mulinum spinosum.note: Neneo, the spiny cushion shrub that dots the wind-scoured Patagonian steppe.

Nepenthes.note: Tropical pitcher plants; the largest hold litres and have caught rats.

Nestor notabilis.note: The kea, the world's only alpine parrot, and one of its cleverest birds.

Nipponia nippon.note: The crested ibis, down to seven birds in the Qinling foothills in 1981 and since recovered.

Ochotona princeps.note: The American pika, haying all summer on talus slopes and retreating uphill as the mountains warm.

Odobenus rosmarus.note: The walrus, raking clams from the Arctic shelf and hauling out on ice with its tusks.

Odocoileus.note: White-tailed and mule deer, the New World's own deer and its commonest large mammals.

Oncorhynchus clarkii.note: The cutthroat trout, whose Bonneville and Lahontan forms are what is left of the fish of the great pluvial lakes.

Oreotragus oreotragus.note: The klipspringer, a small antelope that walks on the tips of its hooves on bare rock.

Orestias.note: Andean pupfish: a species flock of the high-altitude lakes, centred on Titicaca.

Ornithoptera alexandrae.note: Queen Alexandra's birdwing, the largest butterfly, with a wingspan of 28 cm.

Ornithorhynchus anatinus.note: The platypus: egg-laying, venomous, and hunting with its eyes shut by sensing the electric fields of its prey.

Oryx leucoryx.note: The Arabian oryx, white against the sand; extinct in the wild by 1972 and returned from captive herds.

Osphranter rufus.note: The red kangaroo, largest living marsupial, following rain across the arid interior.

Ovis ammon.note: The argali, largest of wild sheep, its horns spiralling to nearly two metres.

Ovis canadensis.note: The bighorn sheep, on desert ranges and Rocky Mountain crags alike.

Pan troglodytes.note: The chimpanzee, our closest living relative, a tool-maker of forest and forest edge.

Pandanus.note: Screw pines on stilt roots, fringing Indo-Pacific shores.

Panthera pardus.note: The leopard, the most adaptable big cat, from rainforest to desert mountain.

Panthera tigris.note: The tiger, from Siberian taiga to Sumatran rainforest.

Paradisaeidae.note: Birds-of-paradise: crows' cousins that, with no predators to fear, turned entirely to display.

Parahyaena brunnea.note: The brown hyena, a shaggy scavenger of the Kalahari and the Namib coast, where it takes seal pups.

Pharomachrus mocinno.note: The resplendent quetzal of the Mesoamerican cloud forest, its tail coverts a metre long.

Phascolarctos cinereus.note: The koala, living on eucalypt leaves too poor and too toxic for almost anything else.

Phoeniconaias minor.note: The lesser flamingo, filtering cyanobacteria from soda lakes caustic enough to burn skin.

Phoenix dactylifera.note: The date palm, the tree that makes an oasis: feet in groundwater, head in the desert sun.

Phragmites australis.note: The common reed, walling lake margins and deltas on every continent but Antarctica.

Phrynocephalus.note: Toad-headed agamas, the small lizards of Central Asian sand and gravel desert up to 5,000 m.

Phyllostachys.note: The timber bamboos of China, mass-flowering and dying back in cycles decades long.

Picea glauca.note: White spruce, the tree that followed the retreating Laurentide ice north.

Picea schrenkiana.note: Schrenk's spruce, which forms the dark forest belt on the north slopes of the Tien Shan.

Pinus longaeva.note: The Great Basin bristlecone pine; individuals close to five thousand years old still stand on dolomite ridges above 3,000 m.

Pinus sibirica.note: The Siberian stone pine, whose nuts feed the taiga from nutcrackers to bears.

Pongo.note: Orangutans, the red apes of Borneo and Sumatra, once found north to China.

Procapra gutturosa.note: The Mongolian gazelle, still migrating in herds of tens of thousands across the eastern steppe.

Propithecus.note: Sifakas: large lemurs that cross open ground in sideways leaps.

Prosopis.note: Mesquite and algarrobo: thorny legume trees with taproots reaching tens of metres to groundwater.

Protea.note: Sugarbushes: the emblem of the Cape fynbos, a fire-dependent heathland with more plant species than any rainforest of its size.

Pseudotsuga menziesii.note: The Douglas-fir, to ninety metres -- the great tree of the Pacific slope.

Psittacus erithacus.note: The grey parrot of the Congo and Guinea forests.

Pteronura brasiliensis.note: The giant otter, two metres long, hunting Amazonian rivers in noisy family groups.

Pudu puda.note: The southern pudu, the world's smallest deer, in the bamboo thickets of the Valdivian forest.

Pusa caspica.note: The Caspian seal, stranded in an inland sea since the Paratethys broke up.

Pusa sibirica.note: The nerpa, the world's only wholly freshwater seal, two thousand kilometres from the nearest sea.

Puya raimondii.note: The queen of the Andes: a bromeliad that grows for eighty years at 4,000 m, flowers once on a ten-metre spike, and dies.

Pygoscelis adeliae.note: The Adelie penguin, nesting on the few ice-free Antarctic shores and feeding on krill under the pack.

Rafflesia.note: A parasite with no leaves, stem or roots, producing the largest single flower on Earth, a metre across and smelling of carrion.

Ravenala madagascariensis.note: The traveller's tree, a giant fan of banana-like leaves pollinated by lemurs.

Rhea americana.note: The greater rhea of the pampas and cerrado.

Rhea pennata.note: Darwin's rhea, the flightless runner of Patagonian steppe and Andean puna.

Rhinoceros unicornis.note: The Indian rhinoceros, armour-plated in folds, of the tall-grass floodplains below the Himalaya.

Rhinopithecus roxellana.note: The golden snub-nosed monkey of the Qinling, living through snowbound winters on lichen and bark.

Rollandia microptera.note: The Titicaca grebe, flightless and found on this one lake system.

Rupicapra rupicapra.note: The chamois, goat-antelope of the Alps, Carpathians and Caucasus.

Sagittarius serpentarius.note: The secretarybird, a long-legged raptor that hunts snakes on foot.

Salvelinus namaycush.note: The lake trout, a cold-water char of the deep glacial lakes left by the Laurentide ice.

Sarcophilus harrisii.note: The Tasmanian devil, largest surviving marsupial carnivore; on the mainland until about 3,000 years ago.

Saxifraga oppositifolia.note: Purple saxifrage, flowering at the northernmost point of land on Earth.

Schoenoplectus californicus.note: Totora, the giant bulrush of Lake Titicaca from which the Uros build boats and floating islands.

Semnopithecus.note: Grey langurs, leaf-eating monkeys from Sri Lanka to 4,000 m in the Himalaya.

Shorea robusta.note: Sal, the dipterocarp that forms the forests of the Himalayan foothills and central India.

Solenodon.note: A venomous, shrew-like relict of Cuba and Hispaniola whose lineage goes back to the age of dinosaurs.

Stercorarius maccormicki.note: The south polar skua, pirate and predator of the penguin colonies, recorded at the Pole itself.

Strigops habroptila.note: The kakapo: flightless, nocturnal, the heaviest parrot, breeding only when the rimu trees mast.

Subglacial microbes.note: Bacteria and archaea living in lakes sealed beneath four kilometres of ice, without light, on minerals ground from the bedrock.

Suricata suricatta.note: The meerkat: a small mongoose of the Kalahari living in co-operative mobs with sentries.

Sus scrofa.note: The wild boar, ploughing forest floors from Portugal to Japan.

Swietenia.note: Mahogany, the emergent timber tree of the Neotropical forest.

Syncerus caffer.note: The African buffalo, in herds of a thousand on the floodplains.

Tapirus bairdii.note: Baird's tapir, the largest native land mammal of Central America.

Tapirus indicus.note: The Malayan tapir, black and white, the only Old World tapir left.

Tarsius.note: Tarsiers: tiny nocturnal primates with eyes each as large as their brain, and the only wholly carnivorous primates.

Taxidea taxus.note: The American badger, digging out ground squirrels across the prairie.

Taxodium distichum.note: The bald cypress, a deciduous conifer standing in blackwater swamps on buttressed trunks and 'knees'.

Tectona grandis.note: Teak, the great timber tree of the monsoon forests, leafless through the dry season.

Tenrec ecaudatus.note: The tailless tenrec, one of a Madagascan radiation that has filled the roles of shrews, hedgehogs and otters.

Tetrao urogallus.note: The capercaillie, the turkey-sized grouse of old conifer forest.

Themeda triandra.note: Red oat grass or kangaroo grass, the fire-adapted dominant of savannas from Africa to Australia.

Tillandsia landbeckii.note: A rootless air plant forming banded 'lawns' on bare Atacama dunes, watered entirely by coastal fog.

Tremarctos ornatus.note: The spectacled bear of the Andean cloud forest, last of the short-faced bears.

Triodia.note: Spinifex: needle-leaved hummock grasses covering a quarter of Australia, and shelter for most of its desert reptiles.

Uromastyx.note: Spiny-tailed lizards: plant-eating desert agamids that block their burrows with a clubbed tail.

Ursus arctos.note: The brown bear, from Spanish mountains across Siberia to Alaska.

Ursus maritimus.note: The polar bear, a brown-bear offshoot that became a marine mammal, hunting seals from the sea ice.

Usnea antarctica.note: A bushy beard lichen, among the largest land organisms of the Antarctic Peninsula.

Vachellia erioloba.note: The camel thorn, the Kalahari's great shade tree, rooted sixty metres down.

Varanus giganteus.note: The perentie, Australia's largest living lizard at over two metres, a hunter of the rocky deserts.

Varanus komodoensis.note: The Komodo dragon, a three-metre monitor that evolved in Australia and survives on a few Indonesian islands.

Victoria amazonica.note: The giant water lily, its ribbed leaves three metres across.

Vombatus ursinus.note: The common wombat, a burrowing grazer with a backward-facing pouch.

Wollemia nobilis.note: The Wollemi pine, known only as a fossil until a hundred trees were found in one canyon near Sydney in 1994.

Yucca brevifolia.note: The Joshua tree of the Mojave, pollinated by a single species of moth; its seeds were once spread by ground sloths.

Zaedyus pichiy.note: The pichi, a small armadillo of cold Patagonian steppe and the only one known to hibernate.

Zaglossus.note: Long-beaked echidnas, worm-eating monotremes of New Guinea's mountain forests.

Zizania palustris.note: Wild rice, the aquatic grass of Great Lakes shallows.

Bubalus depressicornis.note: The anoa, a dwarf forest buffalo barely a metre tall, found only on Sulawesi.

Macrocephalon maleo.note: The maleo, a megapode that buries its eggs in volcanically heated sand and leaves them.

Ailurops ursinus.note: The bear cuscus: a marsupial in Asia, one of the few mammals to cross Wallacea from the Australian side.

Eucalyptus deglupta.note: The rainbow gum, the only eucalypt native north of the equator, its bark peeling in green, orange and purple strips.

Agathis dammara.note: The Sulawesi kauri, a towering araucarian conifer tapped for dammar resin.
